First, we let

$$
L={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{{e}^{2+h}-{e}^{2}}{h}.
$$

Comparing this with the formula for the instantaneous rate of change

$$
{f}^{′}(a)={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h}.
$$

We see that if we let $f(x)={e}^{x}$ and $a=2$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(2) & ={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{f(2+h)-f(2)}{h} \\  & ={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{{e}^{2+h}-{e}^{2}}{h}=L.\end{aligned}
$$

This confirms that $L={f}^{′}(2).$  

Computing the derivative, we have
 

$$
{f}^{′}(x)={e}^{x},\,{f}^{′}(2)={e}^{2},
$$

and therefore we conclude tha $L={e}^{2}.$
